The trouble with the resolution of cliffhangers is that it's extremely difficult to meet or exceed audience expectations.

The first part of the story can focus on breaking everything apart and building to a massive question mark in the story, which is fun and exciting, while the second part has the unenviable task of laboriously putting everything back together again.

Sometimes this can be a bit dry or possibly even boring. The issue with cliffhanger resolutions is that they're very, very easy to get wrong and can often become predictable paint-by-numbers affairs.

The reason for this is because the audience knows that the universe has to be put back together the way it was.

The trap that writers can fall into is turning the second part into the opposite of the first part.

It's far easier, more fun and entertaining for the writers to set up a major dramatic earth-shattering cliffhanger in the first part, but it's much less compelling to watch it all being put back together and undone or fixed up in the second part.

Satisfying cliffhanger payoffs are very tough to achieve. Worst case scenario, if a cliffhanger conclusion is done wrong, the writers can lazily fall back on the tired trope of everything was a dream.

Though I very much doubt that's how Avengers Endgame will resolve the cliffhanger set up in Infinity War.

The film was released in 1975. The movie takes place in the year 2018. The game has become the new national and indeed global pastime.

The game takes place in a large circular arena, like an indoor cycling track, complete with banked walls.

Players traverse the course on either motorbikes or skates. The object is for your team to get possession of the metal ball and get the ball into a goal being defended by the opposition.

It's a rough game, brutal in fact, a real gladiatorial spectacle. James Cahn brilliantly plays Jonathan E, the most famous and successful rollerball player ever.

He plays for the Houston team and he's the undefeated champion of the sport. He's had an incredible career.

But the executives of the sport want him to retire, which Jonathan does not want to do.

Mr. Bartholomew is the chairman of the Energy Corporation and the sponsor of the Houston team.

He tells Jonathan about the purpose of Rollerball as a cultural spectacle. It has a definite social purpose.

Because nations of the world are bankrupt and gone, even the corporate wars are over.

But a small elite managing everything on the planet, energy, housing, transport, food, communication, luxury, they make the decisions, on a global basis, for the common good.

Anita Sarkeesian would no doubt find that deeply misogynistic. Anyway, this is a side-scrolling platform beat-em-up, complete with magics, undead monsters, and of course, the ability for your character to transform into different beasts with their own unique strengths.

Two-player mode made this game a hell of a lot easier. This was immensely challenging when played alone.

Number 8, NHL Hockey 91. This was a fast-paced and incredibly fun sports title that seems to have been largely overlooked in the console's history.

The graphics and sound effects were decent for the time, but it was the frenetic gameplay, fights, attention to detail with respect to the rules, and player physics that really immersed you.

I personally could... I didn't see the appeal of John Madden football, but I sunk a ridiculous amount of time into this game.

Today I'm going to be reviewing Snowpiercer, the 2013 post-apocalyptic film, not the TV series of the same name.

It stars Chris Evans as Curtis Everett, as well as Song Kang Ho as Min Soong, Ed Harris as Wilford, Jamie Bell as Edgar and John Hurt as Gilliam.

After a failed environmental solution, shall we say, causes a major catastrophe and creates a new ice age and wipes out most life on Earth?

All that remains of humanity now takes refuge on a train that's circumnavigating the Earth, like a perpetually moving Noah's Ark on rails.

It's 2031, so not that far away. The passengers are segregated on the train into different social classes, with the poor at the rear of the train and the wealthy and privileged elite at the front, like Titanic, steerage, second class, first class, except the segregation is horizontal and not vertical, because this is a train obviously, and not a boat.

The poor at the rear of the train live under brutal military police state conditions and make do with processed ration food, some kind of jelly protein blocks, which are actually made from... insects.

Hmm, interesting. The population of this part of the train are routinely subjected to violent oppression at the hands of the guards.

It's certainly an interesting concept to have all of humanity now living on a train with its own cultural norms and class-based structure.

It certainly makes for an original world-building premise. Curtis, Edgar and Gilliam are involved in the process of organizing a carefully coordinated rebellion, one they're hopeful of pulling off after they realise that the guards guns have no bullets, because apparently there's no bullets left, so they're led to believe.

The plan is to get through the security barriers and break a man named Minsu out of prison.

He's a security specialist and should be able to help them reach the front of the train.

pool section, medical facilities, but I think the one truly eyebrow-raising moment in the film for me was the twist at the end where Wilfred explains to Curtis that revolutions such as the one Curtis has just undertaken are sometimes used as a drastic means of population reduction in order to keep the population in sustainable balance.

Coherence is a film I only recently got around to watching and it's one I highly recommend to you if you haven't seen it.

It's from 2013 and it was directed by James Ward Burkett who developed the story with his friend Alex Munigan who also stars in the film incidentally.

It's a micro budget sci-fi movie that was shot over five nights almost entirely in Burkett's living room and it's a fantastic piece of indie filmmaking.

I mean the budget was just fifty thousand dollars and it shows what can be done with a great vision, talent and ingenuity.

As they say necessity is the mother of invention. It is a sci-fi film but it's also one of these psychological thriller horror movies.

It's quite unnerving and creepy in places and it's phenomenally executed. Burkett gets back to first principles, bare-bones filmmaking, keeping everything simple, no elaborate filmmaking crew and no script.

The cast of actors improvised their dialogue drawing only on note cards that Burkett and Munugian would give them each day.

Each actor had an outline of the main points they needed to hit with their characters but they had no idea what the other actors had received on their note cards that day.

This meant that the reactions and surprises were genuine and as natural as possible.

So this film has been compared to Primer in that it's a low-budget sci-fi movie with extremely naturalistic performance.

And I have to say, hats off to the cast. These eight actors do an incredible job and it must be an improv actor's dream to make a film like this because they really have to fully throw themselves into their characters completely.

Although there was no script, Birkett and Manuagian did have a treatment and story outline, so it wasn't made up as they went along, but they also were obviously relying on the abilities of the actors to carry the film and they certainly did that.

Improvisation was definitely the right choice for this film because it makes events feel grounded in reality and the characters reactions to all of the craziness feels believable because there's an unpredictability about their interactions which perfectly mirrors the unpredictability of the events taking place in the story.

Coherence is essentially a variation on a haunted house themed movie but wrapped up in a unique quantum mechanics sci-fi explanation.

I think if all the dialogue had been scripted, the film and its concept would have lacked the immersion and grounded quality that makes the whole thing work in the first place.

Given the subject matter and style of movie that Coherence is, entirely scripted dialogue could have potentially caused the film to fall into predictability, cliche and even over the top melodrama.

Instead, we get a masterclass in what great actors can do when a creative and visionary director has faith in their abilities.

And just a reminder that this movie was made for only $50,000 and yeah sure it's a small film, it's an intimate movie that takes place primarily in one location but it's proof to Hollywood once again that you don't need hundreds of... of dollars to make a great movie and tell a fantastic story.

I can't recommend Coherence highly enough and I think it goes very well with a movie like Primer.

Now, traditionally superhero films have followed the tried and tested formulas of a flawed individual realizing often reluctantly, after careful reflection, that they must change as a person or they must be broken down, face their fears and dig deep within themselves to either right a past wrong and seek redemption or become a better version of themselves.

They are forever changed by the trauma or crisis they faced, be it personal or external, or they must learn to cope with the responsibility of newfound superhuman abilities and make use of them for good, or they must learn to overcome a darkness within them and channel it for good.

Either way, we as the audience respond to these kinds of stories because at their core there's something virtuous and aspirational about them and they speak to something within our human nature.

Tony Stark was an arrogant narcissist who had to come to a painful personal realization of the consequences of his actions, that Stark Industries was not a force for good in the world, that he was arming nefarious regimes and innocent people were getting caught in the crossfire.

Stranger Things has all the attributes and potential to be a Netflix cult classic.

It caught my eye earlier this year and like many people I was instantly hooked. Say what you will about Hollywood movie writing, but television writers are absolutely crushing it when it comes to creativity and quality of scripted drama.

Major spoilers lie ahead by the way, so be warned. This is a sci-fi horror series based during the 1980s, which was a very refreshing decision indeed.

The authenticity and nostalgia element alone and homage to John Carpenter films and movies like The Goonies makes this series visually, thematically and tonally very different.

So what's it all about? Well it's based in a small town in Indiana. Incidentally, in the same year I was born, 1983, a young boy named Will Byers goes missing in the woods after being chased by some kind of strange alien-like creature and transported into another realm.

The main plot concerns the primary characters of his mother Joyce, a police officer Jim Hopper, his brother and his three young friends trying to find him.

In the meantime, a young girl dubbed Eleven who possesses psychokinetic abilities and seems to have lived her life as a science experiment has shown up and she's escaped from a shady government agency looking to find her.

Said agency also seemed to have at least been investigating the alternative universe where Will now resides.

Little is known about who or what they are or their motivations, but suffice to say they certainly don't give the appearance of being a force for good.

I won't go into too much detail and turn this into a full review of the series, more a kind of thoughts and opinions piece.

Firstly, the series has been compared to Lost in terms of the show's intrigue, viewer immersion and utterly compelling and addictive narrative.

You simply have to know what happens in the next episode. I watched the entire eight episode first season in two days.

I would have watched it in one, but I had things to do like eating and sleeping.

And almost every character on the show has their own baggage they must overcome, none more so than Will's mother Joyce, played by Winona Ryder.

Ryder does an incredible job with Joyce. This character reminded me of Ripley from Aliens.

No one believes her son is trying to speak to her from another dimension. She knows she's not crazy, but her sanity is being seriously questioned as the reality around her and the helplessness she feels for her lost son begin to take their toll.

Joyce is perhaps the bravest and most selfless character of them all, as she slowly battles her own paranoia and fracturing mental state while risking everything to save Will.

Steve Harrington could have been... another cardboard cutout bad boy jock type character.

This film is 90 minutes long and is solely focused on the battle between David and the truck driver on the road.

So I finally sat down and watched Avengers Endgame for the second time, and generally speaking, I still maintain that it's a good film, although not as slick as Infinity War.

However, having had a chance to view it again, I've been able to more thoroughly identify the issues that the film has, of which there are quite a few.

My frustration with Endgame is that it could have been an absolute classic. Instead, it's a bit messy in places, and it failed to do some of the characters the justice they deserved.

In my review of Endgame from earlier this year, I explained some of the issues I had with the film, such as the fact that it suffered from being bogged down by far too much exposition, which is often common for cliffhanger resolution stories, and especially in stories involving complicated time travel plot devices, and I wasn't happy with how Natasha Romanoff was killed off.

Also, I lamented the poor treatment of Thor. He becomes an alcoholic and a fat emotional wreck, who loses his way, and it's all played for laughs, thus compromising the character and turning him into a bit of a joke.

I had other complaints with the film also, but my second viewing of the film has allowed me to pinpoint the primary gripe I have with Endgame, the conclusion, specifically the final showdown with Thanos, how it was handled, and how he was defeated.

I think I've got a perspective here that many people may not consider when it comes to how the MCU's biggest villain was finally overcome.

Caden may be a character who found life pointless, to the point of pursuing an unprecedented form of escapism, but that doesn't mean the film also had to feel equally as pointless by the end.

Those are my thoughts on Synecdoche, New York.

My dystopian future series continues this time with a film I've been asked to review more times than any other. A film that's garnered a cult following in recent years and some believed to be a cautionary tale for human civilization. The 2006 Mike Judge film Idiocracy, starring Luke Wilson, Maya Rudolph and Dax Shepard. I'll provide a general summary of the plot, but of course my primary focus will be exploring the film's central themes. Like many movies that develop a cult following, Idiocracy was not financially successful. From its $2-4 million budget, it brought in a box office return of less than $500,000 because it wasn't screened in many theatres. For whatever reason, Fox decided not to heavily promote the movie and largely abandoned it, leaving it to develop interest through word of mouth. The film explores the concept of anti-intellectualism through dysgenics. The perpetuation of lower quality and disadvantageous genes and characteristics in offspring over time. The average IQ of the population declines dramatically, leading to stagnation and widespread societal, economic and cultural problems. The opening of the movie has become iconic at this point, perfectly explaining what happens when a large percentage of the population becomes dependent on the welfare state, and when competition for survival is no longer optimal. The success and decadence achieved through massive amounts of free resources generated through the tax system in a capitalist society means

that over time evolution no longer selects for intelligence, strength, excellence and fitness and instead simply favours those who breed the most.

In the opening sequence, a young professional couple are seen being interviewed over several years.

They both have very high IQs of 138 and 141 respectively and they're actually considering having children someday but are cautious about it and wish to plan their careers and save money for the future.

are seen being interviewed over several years.

They both have very high IQs of 138 and 141 respectively and they're actually considering having children someday but are cautious about it and wish to plan their careers and save money for the future.

This is juxtaposed with a low IQ hick family who are likely supported through the welfare state and the father breeds with multiple women with reckless abandon, passing on the same mindset to his low IQ son.

Before too long, a massive family tree emerges comprised of many illegitimate low IQ offspring while the high IQ couple never end up breeding.

This of course fits neatly into RK selection theory. The professional couple wish to have a small family so they can provide a high level of parental investment thus ensuring their children are given the best possible opportunity to compete, survive and thrive.

However, that's a K selected strategy, ideal for when resources are scarce. But when resources are abundant, the reproductive strategy that succeeds in an environment is an R strategy.

So instead of breeding like wolves, which is to say breeding less and investing time to train and prepare your high quality offspring for life, the masses will instead begin to breed more like rabbits.

Breeding large... amounts of offspring as fast as possible. Those same offspring will then begin engaging in sexual activity younger and will in turn have large families of their own.

Why? Because rabbits breed in such a fashion because their food supply, grass, is endless and therefore competing for resources is a waste of time.

Monogamy is a waste of time, just like fitness is unnecessary. Similarly here, the hicks breed in greater number because the welfare state provides the illusion of infinite resources.

In truth, resources are merely abundant, they're not infinite. The welfare state will run out as the reproductive rate of the species reaches the carrying capacity of the environment.

In 2007 a UK High Court ruled that an inconvenient truth contained nine major scientific errors. The film wasn't banned for being shown in schools or anything, but was ruled that it must be shown with a guidance note in order to prevent political indoctrination. Here are some of the things that the film got wrong according to the High Court ruling. Mr. Gore claims that a sea level rise of up to 20 feet would be caused by melting of either West Antarctica or Greenland in the near future. The judge said this is distinctly alarmist and part of Mr. Gore's wake-up call. He agreed that if Greenland melted it would release this amount of water but only after and over millennia. The Armageddon scenario he predicts, insofar as it suggests that sea level rises of seven meters might occur in the immediate future, is not in line with the scientific consensus. The film claims that low-lying inhabited Pacific atolls are being inundated because of anthropogenic global warming, but the judge ruled there was no evidence of any evacuation having yet happened. The documentary speaks of global warming shutting down the ocean conveyor, the process by which the Gulf Stream is carried over the North Atlantic to Western Europe, citing the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change.

The 1972 Danish-American film, a dystopian sci-fi movie called ZPG, also known as Zero Population Growth, the film stars Oliver Reed and Geraldine Chaplin, and depicts a brutal totalitarian world similar to Huxley's Brave New World, or the world in Orwell's 1984, where the oppressive government tightly controls the population numbers by implementing a ban on reproduction for several decades.

The film follows a trend of movies released in the 1970s concerned with population control, such as films that I've previously reviewed like Logan's Run and Soylent Green.

ZPG was directed by Michael Campus and written by Frank Defolita and Max Elric. The earth in this movie is not only overpopulated but entirely polluted, and going outside requires a person to wear an oxygen mask to withstand the extreme smog in the atmosphere.

Most plant and animal life are now extinct. The population all wear these dark blue jumpsuits, like in 1984, or the dehumanising uniforms we saw in Equilibrium.

It's a bland, grey world, devoid of fun and spontaneity, and everything the people have, including their oxygen, is rationed by the constantly visible and intrusive government, which makes public announcements on a regular basis every day, and the food of this horrid future is some kind of paste that comes out of a tube.

Mmm, delightful. The film follows primary characters Russ, played by Oliver Reed, and Carol, played by Geraldine Chaplin.

So I'm looking forward to getting back into the Orville, having been generally impressed with the show's first season.

I'll be doing my season 2 review in multiple parts. Today, we're looking at the first three episodes.

Now, I'll be honest, these first three episodes are a bit of a mixed bag. By no means are the episodes bad, but I'm still getting the impression that this series hasn't truly hit its stride, and it just feels that creatively, the Orville hasn't achieved its full potential.

The season opener is called Jellojah, which has been described as a character-driven story, and that's essentially what it is.

As a season premiere, it does a pretty decent job of reintroducing all of the main characters, so that newcomers to the show can get up to speed on everything quite quickly, and in that sense, it works very well.

All of the main ensemble get a reasonable amount of things to do. The episode begins with Ed drowning his sorrows in the mess hall.

He's still hurting over the breakup with Kelly from last season, though I like Captain Mercer quite a bit, and Seth MacFarlane does a solid job as the show's lead.

The character can be a bit... beta at times. The needy, lovesick puppy thing is not an endearing quality, and in his conversations with Kelly, where he's basically begging for her to take him back, he just comes off as weak and massively insecure.

When it comes to being a captain, he's large and in charge. When it comes to his relationship with Grayson, he's a bit emasculated.

Long story short, their story is the primary plot thread of the episode. There are five stories in this episode.

Four of them are anchored... to the Bortus B plot, which is that he must return to Mokkles because he has to urinate.

Something that Mokkles only do once per year. And it's followed by a celebration known as Jellosia.

As I'm sure you're now well aware, Star Wars hasn't exactly been in the best health since Disney purchased Lucasfilm, but having said that, it hasn't all been bad.

2016's Rogue One, A Star Wars Story, was actually a pretty decent prequel film, and it also has a very impressive visual effects highlight, which was the digital likeness of the late Peter Cushing as Grand Moff Tarkin.

But as I've mentioned some time ago, I'm not really in favour of deceased actors being brought back using CGI, even if their estate and or family have given permission for filmmakers to do so.

I personally think the dead should be allowed to rest. We have no idea if they would have actually agreed to appear in such films.

I don't know why they just didn't cast a new actor in the role. It makes more sense to me.

This trend of digital necromancy, as it's been called, is just creepy in my opinion.

Anyway, Peter Cushing's likeness was an impressive technical feat, but nothing more.

I still don't agree with it. Now, having said that, I am more sympathetic to this kind of thing if an actor died part way through a film, and they need to use their CGI likeness in order to finish the film.

That's different, because the actor actually consented to being in the film. in the first place, like for example Oliver Reed in Gladiator, they had to use CGI there, and of course Paul Walker in Fast and Furious 7.

But when it's an entirely new production, there's no need to digitally resurrect someone.

We recently saw another digital likeness of a deceased actor in Alien Romulus, where Ian Holmes' face and voice were digitally recreated.

But it turns out the use of Peter Cushing's likeness in Rogue One is being challenged legally.

This article is from IGN. Lucasfilm sued for recreating Grand Moff Tarkin actor Peter Cushing's image in Rogue One, A Star Wars Story.

Cushing died in 1994. Disney's subsidiary Lucasfilm is being sued over its recreation of Grand Moff Tarkin actor Peter Cushing's image in Rogue One, A Star Wars Story.

As reported by The Times, a friend of Cushing has alleged Disney did not have permission to recreate the actor's image with special effects for Rogue One.

Disney tried and failed to have the case dismissed for a second time on September 9th, 2024.

The plaintiff, Kevin Francis, is suing Lucasfilm through his film company, Tyburn Film Productions, and also brought claims against Rogue One producer Lunac Heavy Industries, the late executors of Cushing's estate and Cushing's agency, Associated International Management.

Francis claimed he must give authorization for any recreation of Cushing's image, following an agreement made between him and the actor in 1993, one year before his death at age 81.

Lucasfilm claimed it didn't think it needed permission to recreate Cushing's image due to his original contract for Star Wars, the 1977 film which became Star Wars Episode 4, A New Hope, and The Nature of the Special Effects.

It also paid around $37,000 to Cushing's estate after being contacted by his agent about the recreation.

On September 9th, Deputy High Court Judge Tom Mitchinson dismissed the appeal, stating that the case should go to trial.

I'm also not persuaded that the case is unarguable to the standard required to give summary judgment or to strike it out, he added.

Death on the Nile is of course based on the 1937 novel by Agatha Christie, a Hercule Poirot murder mystery story.

I have to say I'm a sucker for murder mysteries and I always enjoyed the David Suchet version of Poirot.

My mother was a big fan of the TV series and the books so I grew up with Poirot on the television quite a lot.

Kenneth Branagh plays the role in this film which is a sequel to the 2017 adaptation of Murder on the Orient Express.

He directed both films also. It took a little bit of an adjustment to get used to Branagh in the role rather than Suchet but I really like Branagh's interpretation, different from Suchet's take but still recognizably Poirot in his own right.

And I have to say credit where credit is due because Branagh really does bring a strong sense of gravitas and charisma to the character of Poirot, capturing the characters whimsical and sometimes humorous idiosyncrasies while also brilliantly portraying his serious intellectual genius.

This film is a throwback to the whodunit murder mystery period based classics where a large ensemble cast of colorful characters are stuck in one primary location, in this case a boat and they are all possible suspects in a murder investigation which only Poirot's brilliant deductive reasoning skills can solve.

So structurally it's quite similar to Murder on the Orient Express. although it's not quite as endearing or emotionally compelling as that story, I think.

I won't offer major spoilers for this film, but the 2017 version of Orient Express was very well executed.

It had a charm and genuine sense of intrigue. Death on the Nile offers much the same thing again, although it doesn't make quite the same impact as the first film.

Today we're going to look at something a little bit different. A review of what I affectionately refer to as a lost episode of Star Trek.

Star Trek Borg was produced in 1996 by Simon and Shuster which puts its release about a month before Star Trek First Contact was released.

This is actually an interactive movie. It's a point and click video game from the 90s era when Full Motion Video was all the rage, written by Hilary Bader and directed by Star Trek veteran James L.

Conway who directed multiple episodes of TNG, DS9, Voyager and Enterprise. The movie was filmed on actual Star Trek sets, specifically Voyager sets, and it makes use of actual Star Trek props and costumes.

The game features the acting talents of franchise veterans John Delancey as Q and Majel Barrett as the voice of the ship's computer.

The story really is centred around Q as the main character for the first time and John Delancey just chews the scenery.

He is wonderful as Q and the writing in this episode is fantastic. It feels like a proper extra long episode of one of the shows because the duration of the film itself is about an hour.

So the game works by allowing the player to make decisions at certain points in the film by clicking on items on screen.

They could be buttons on a tricorder, a phaser, a computer console for example. I will say that the gameplay isn't particularly sophisticated by today's standards.

If you make the wrong decision you can die, but Q will always reset you back to just before that moment so you can try again.

There's only one narrative path in the game, leading to only one ending, so the game doesn't allow you to stray too far away from the story for very long before pulling you back to the main plot thread.

What is AI? Legislation is still evolving when it comes to artificial intelligence, specifically content generated by AI and the distinctions between purely AI-generated content and content that is classified as AI-assisted.

It is an absolute grey area in some respects because AI tools are encroaching into applications more and more.

For example, certain graphic design applications are increasingly incorporating AI tools.

Where once you might have to manually and painstakingly remove a background from a photograph in order to isolate a person in the foreground, now some AI tools will do this with a single click.

Over the next few years, you are likely going to see significantly more AI functionality in the likes of video editing applications, allowing for more automation in workflow and previously laborious editing and video processing tasks.

There are a lot of concerns about AI replacing creative jobs, the likes of writers, artists and so forth, but there may have been some unnecessary alarm about this.

For starters, AI-generated content cannot be copyrighted. As a result, it is considered public domain content. content is a different matter, however.

Technically, if you've created something and used AI to augment it or revise it in some way, that's okay.

You can still retain legal authorship of that content. You can copyright it. But sometimes the definition of what is AI-assisted can be a bit unclear.

As I'm not an expert on this matter, however, it's best to consult a legal authority on this.

For writing, AI language models can be a great way to help generate ideas or assist in detecting grammar, punctuation, spelling mistakes, as well as editing, but I don't believe that AI should ever be used to actually write something for you, assuming you want to actually be the owner of that content.

Personally, I don't think we should be outsourcing our creative abilities to a machine.

Although AI can write very nice literary prose, it lacks the ability to generate original ideas because it can only really synthesize and riff on previously created works.

Adams. Of course, most people will know Leslie Nielsen from his role as Frank Drebben from the Police Squad TV series, and subsequent Naked Gun films, as well as comedy films like Airplane.

But he's nonetheless a very strong leading man in the role of Commander Adams. In the distant future, mankind has sent the flying saucer C-57D to the planet Altair IV to find out what happened to a lost Earth expedition from 20 years ago.

The ship makes use of hyperdrive technology capable of faster-than-light travel.

For a film made 64 years ago, the visual effects are fantastic, very impressive, and it wouldn't be until 2001 A Space Odyssey in 1968 that they would be surpassed.

The universe of Forbidden Planet and its technologies, parameters, and rules, it's also very well defined.

It's very well developed. Despite some very corny dialogue in places, some cringy scenes between Alta and the crew, this is generally a fairly clever cerebral move.

The sets are very impressive and the fantastic production values mean that the film has dated very well.

The film definitely has a Star Trek original series feel to it. It feels like a big budget feature length episode of Star Trek.

And that should probably come as no surprise given that Gene Roddenberry drew inspiration for Star Trek from this film.
